name: ai.swapwire/contractor-licenses
title: Swapwire
description: California contractor license checks (CSLB): status, bond, workers' comp, quote matching.

tools.name: get_license
tools.description: Full record for one contractor license by number: status, license types, bond, insurance, workers' comp, discipline, complaints and citations where published, city permits, and the agency source link. California is the default; pass state for others. Use this when you have a license number, or after search_licenses to read a match in full (use the id it returns).

license_number.description: License number as the agency prints it, or the id from search_licenses, e.g. "1154967" (CA) or "CGC047089" (FL).

state.description: Two-letter state code. Default CA. License records: CO, CT, FL, IL, KS, MN, NY, OR, PA, TX, VA, WA. City permit records only (record_type permits_only, no state license data): AZ, GA, HI, LA, MA, MI, NC, NV, OH, TN.

tools.name: search_licenses
tools.description: Search contractor licenses (California by default; pass state for others) three ways. (1) By business name, as written on a quote, invoice, truck or website: typos, word forms (plumber/plumbing), missing words and Inc/LLC are handled, and other names on the CSLB record are matched too (other_business_names lists the ones that are business names). Each match has a match_level (exact, strong, partial) and says what it matched on. (2) By license number. (3) With no name, by trade and/or city to list licensed contractors. The trade can be a description of the job ("my AC is blowing warm air", "sewage backing up"); read_as says how it was read. Lists: clear licenses only by default, in a shuffled order fixed until the next data refresh, 10 per page, up to 5 pages. Lists are not rankings or recommendations. A name match is not proof of identity, so give the user the license number and ask them to confirm it with the contractor. With no state, the state is read from the city ("Seattle, WA", a ZIP, or a city only one state's records list), and a name with no close California match is tried in every state. A question ("is 50% upfront legal", "contractor took my deposit") is not searched: mode is question, with guides that answer it.

name.description: Business name or part of it, e.g. "Diamond Plumbing". Leave out to list by trade and/or city.

license.description: CSLB license number, if you have one.

city.description: City or ZIP code, e.g. "Oakland", "Oakland, CA" or "94704".

trade.description: Trade in plain words or a CSLB code, e.g. "plumbing", "furnace", "water heater", "sewer line", "C-36".

status.description: For lists: clear (default) or all, which includes suspended and other licenses.

work.description: California lists only: a kind of work from city permits, e.g. "water heater", "heat pump", "sewer". Lists only contractors with San Francisco permits for that work in the last five years.

state.description: Two-letter state code. Default CA. License records: CO, CT, FL, IL, KS, MN, NY, OR, PA, TX, VA, WA. City permit records only (record_type permits_only, no state license data): AZ, GA, HI, LA, MA, MI, NC, NV, OH, TN.

tools.name: check_document
tools.description: Check whether a contractor's quote, invoice, contract, business card, ad or truck photo matches a California license in this dataset. Send the document as text, as a PNG or JPEG image (base64), or both, plus the license number to check against (if the text shows a license number from the dataset, it is used). Returns a verdict (consistent, number_only, mismatch or unclear; number_only means only the license number matched, which anyone could copy), whether the business name and license number on the document match the record, whether the work described falls outside the license's classifications, whether the down payment asked for is over California's limit ($1,000 or 10% of the price, whichever is less), and the license's status, bond and workers' comp checks. The verdict is a reading of the document, not proof. The document is read by TypeSafe's Jev model and is not stored by Swapwire; remove a homeowner's personal details before sending if you can.

license_number.description: CSLB license number to check against, digits only. Optional if the text shows it.

text.description: The document's text, e.g. a pasted quote or ad. Up to 20,000 characters.

image_base64.description: A photo or scan of the document, base64-encoded PNG or JPEG, up to 5 MB.

image_format.description: Format of image_base64, if it can't be detected.

tools.name: get_area_stats
tools.description: Counts for each county and trade in the dataset: licenses, how many carry workers' comp insurance or are exempt, how many have a suspension code, median years licensed and how many were issued in the last two years. Useful for saying whether one contractor's record is typical.

tools.name: get_prices
tools.description: Median and middle half (25th to 75th percentile) of what common home jobs cost, from two kinds of public record. (1) Rebate, loan and incentive program records in Oregon, New York, Massachusetts, Connecticut and Delaware: installed cost of heat pumps, solar, battery storage and weatherization, statewide and by county or city. (2) City permit files in 23 US cities and counties (San Francisco, Los Angeles, Seattle, Portland, Austin, Miami-Dade and others): the job value declared on the permit for water heaters (tank, tankless, heat pump), heat pumps, mini splits, furnaces, air conditioners, sewer lines, re-pipes, roof replacements, electrical panels, solar, EV chargers and kitchen and bath remodels, kept to single-job permits at one home. Each permit series gives value_listed_share, the share of the job's permits that list a value at all; where low_value_coverage is true (under a quarter), the median is not the typical job, so do not quote it as one. A declared permit valuation is the applicant's estimate, not a paid price, and often runs low; say so when you quote one. Job words such as "hot water heater", "sewer line" or "AC" and city or county names ("Portland" also finds Multnomah County) are understood. Use it to tell a user whether a quote is in the usual range, and cite the source.

job.description: The job, e.g. "water heater", "sewer line", "AC", "heat pump", "roof", "solar", "weatherization".

area.description: City or county, e.g. "Seattle", "Oakland" or "Multnomah". Default: statewide program series and every city's permit series.

tools.name: get_rules
tools.description: Answers rules questions homeowners ask before hiring, for one state: how much a contractor may ask up front (deposit_limit), when a state license is needed (license_threshold), what an unlicensed handyman may do, including electrical or plumbing (handyman_exemption), whether a job needs a permit (permit_needed: give job, e.g. "water heater", and city), whether a homeowner can pull their own permit (who_can_pull_permits), required bonds and insurance, what a contract must include and the right to cancel (contract_requirements), and the official license lookup (license_lookup). Each answer is short, with its key numbers, conditions, exceptions, an official source URL for every fact, the date it was checked and a Swapwire guide link. status not_verified means Swapwire could not confirm it from an official source: send the user to the agency linked, do not guess. Permits are mostly city rules: the answer gives the state baseline and, for cities where Swapwire has permit records, the city's permit portal. States: CA, AZ, CO, CT, FL, GA, HI, IL, KS, LA, MA, MI, MN, NC, NV, NY, OH, OR, PA, TN, TX, VA, WA. Leave topic out for a one-line answer on every topic. General information, not legal advice.

state.description: Two-letter state code or state name, e.g. "CA" or "Texas". Optional when city names a city Swapwire has permit rules for.

topic.description: Which rule. Leave out for a summary of every topic.

job.description: For permit_needed: the job, in plain words or one of water_heater, hvac_replacement, roof, electrical_panel, fence, deck, bathroom_remodel.

city.description: For permit_needed: the city or county, e.g. "Seattle". Returns its permit portal and any job rules from the city's own pages.
